834.title: Far-off sangats
834.hook: early sangats grew in Kabul, Dhaka and Patna, sending offerings and receiving letters
834.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Takht Sri Patna Sahib as Guru Gobind Singh's birthplace, and gurdwaras in places the Gurus visited keep the memory of the early sangats that gathered there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a roll call of the Gurus' Muslim friends, from Mardana to Rai Kalha. Your line: friends in every faith. Today, Sikhs who lived very far from the Guru.

Anandpur, and a caravan coming in from the northwest, over the mountain passes, dusty and tired. Tradition says it's the sangat of Kabul, bringing gifts for the Guru, among them a fine canopy. They've traveled a very long way to stand in his presence for a little while. Then they'll turn around and make the whole journey again, home to a city where the Guru may never set foot. Today: far-off sangats.
screen: `A CARAVAN FROM KABUL.` → `GIFTS FOR THE GURU.` → `THEN THE LONG ROAD HOME.`

segments.voice: Sangat means the company, the gathered community. A listener might assume the Sikhs of the Gurus' time all lived around Punjab, within a few days' walk. Tradition tells a wider story. Guru Nanak traveled far, and where he went, people remembered. Later Gurus traveled too. Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur journeyed east through Patna and on to Dhaka and Assam, and sangats in those places kept his memory and their gatherings going after he left. Sikhs remember Patna, on the Ganges, as the place where Guru Gobind Singh was born and spent his early childhood, cared for by the sangat there. To the northwest, there was Kabul. So how did a sangat a long journey away stay close to a Guru it might never see? Three ways run through the stories. First, they gave. Far-off Sikhs sent offerings, a share of their earnings, carried by travelers and representatives to the Guru's court. Second, they came. Some, like the Kabul sangat, made the long trip themselves when they could. Third, they listened. Letters went out from the Guru to these sangats, read aloud when they gathered. That's tomorrow's story, so we'll leave the letters sealed for now. Distance didn't make these Sikhs second-class. In the tellings, their gatherings are sangats in full: singing the Gurus' hymns, keeping their own kitchens, and sending their love across mountains and rivers. A sangat, in this story, isn't measured by how close it sits to the center. It's measured by whether it keeps gathering.

Your line: far off, still close. Mountains between, and still one sangat. Day eight hundred thirty-four, done.

835.title: The Gurus' letters
835.hook: the Gurus sent signed letters to sangats, some still kept today
835.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning and the hymn read from the page is called the hukamnama; the daily hukamnama from the Harmandir in Amritsar is widely shared, and historic hukamnamas of the Gurus are kept with honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the far-off sangats of Kabul, Dhaka and Patna, who gave, came and listened. Your line: far off, still close. Today, we open the letters we left sealed.

A bundle wrapped in cloth, in a family's keeping or a gurdwara's care. Inside, an old sheet of paper, the ink faded, the creases gone soft. At the top, tradition says, a mark linked to the Guru's own hand. Below it, lines addressed to a sangat in a faraway place, by name: a blessing, a thank-you, a request or two. Long ago it was carried in to a gathering and read aloud so that everyone could hear. Then someone folded it, and decided it would be kept. Today's word: hukamnama.
screen: `AN OLD LETTER, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `ADDRESSED TO A SANGAT BY NAME.` → `READ ALOUD, THEN KEPT.`

segments.voice: A hukamnama is a letter of hukam, the Guru's command, sent to a sangat. Hukam is a big word in Sikh teaching. At the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, in Japji, Guru Nanak teaches that everything is within the divine hukam, the order of things, and nothing stands outside it. So a hukamnama was never just mail. It carried the Guru's word to people who might never hear his voice. What did the letters say? Tradition and the surviving letters show a mix that's surprisingly human. They bless the sangat. They thank it for offerings already sent. They ask for particular things the Guru's court needed. They tell Sikhs to come when they can, to keep gathering, to live as Sikhs. Some carry the Guru's own signature or mark at the top. And some of these letters are still kept today, held by families and gurdwaras with deep honor, because a letter like that is a link to the Guru's own hand. Here's the part that reaches into the present. Today, in gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning and a hymn from the open page is read out. That reading is also called the hukamnama, the day's word from the Guru. At the Harmandir in Amritsar, the day's hukamnama is shared far beyond its walls. So the far-off sangat still waits for its letter. It just arrives every morning now, from the open page.

836.title: The people close
836.hook: the story was never only ten men; it was a whole sangat
836.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the family, companions and friends of the Gurus in kirtan, in katha and in the stories told at gurdwaras, and the sangat, the gathered community, is central to Sikh worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hukamnama, the Guru's letter to a far-off sangat, read aloud and kept. Your line: letters that last. Today, a look at everyone in this long stretch.

A painting of a Guru's court. The Guru sits at the center, under a canopy, and that's where the eye goes first. But stay with it a moment longer. At the edges are other figures. Someone waving the chaur. A musician with an instrument. A woman at the side. A man carrying water. An old man with a white beard. A visitor in a Sufi's cap. Each figure was painted by someone who thought they belonged in the picture. The center only makes sense because of the edges. Today: the people close.
screen: `A PAINTING OF THE COURT.` → `THE EYE GOES TO THE CENTER.` → `THE EDGES ARE FULL OF PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Lately we've been looking at the edges of the painting. Start with family. Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu, with their love and worry. Bebe Nanaki, the sister who stood by her brother. Mata Sulakhni, steady at home. Mata Khivi, with her generous kitchen. Bibi Amro, whose song changed a life. Bibi Bhani, who held the stool steady. Mata Ganga, Mata Nanaki, Bibi Viro, Mata Gujri. Mata Jito, Mata Sundari, Mata Sahib Kaur. Then the servants and companions. Baba Buddha, who served Guru after Guru. Bhai Gurdas, who was tested too. Bhai Bidhi Chand, a thief turned true. Kirpa Ram, who came back to serve. Daya Singh and the rest of the five, the Panj Pyare. Sangat Singh, who took the Guru's place. Moti Ram Mehra with warm milk. Mai Bhago, who led them back. Bhai Mani Singh, the steady scribe. Bhai Jaita, called the Guru's own son. And the friends: Mian Mir, Budhu Shah, Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, the Nawab of Malerkotla, Todar Mal, Rai Kalha. And the far-off sangats waiting for letters. Gurbani has a word for this. Sangat, the company, and sat sangat, the true company. Guru Nanak asks, on Ang 72, how the true company is known, and answers: it's where the one Name is praised. That's a paraphrase. The Gurus' story was never ten men alone on a stage. It was a gathering, and the gathering is part of the teaching. Next, the path turns to a hard stretch for the Khalsa, and it begins at Nanded, with an ascetic who will become a servant.

837.title: Madho Das the ascetic
837.hook: at Nanded the Guru meets a Bairagi ascetic who becomes Banda, the servant
837.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the meeting of Guru Gobind Singh and Madho Das at Nanded as the beginning of Banda Singh Bahadur's story, and remember that he first named himself the Guru's banda, his servant.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sat sangat, the true company: the family, servants and friends around the Gurus. Your line was a whole sangat. Today a new stretch begins, and it opens far from Punjab.

A hermitage by a river at Nanded, deep in the south. Its master is away. His disciples keep the place the way he likes it, and one thing above all: nobody sits on his cot. Then a traveler arrives with his Sikhs, walks in, and sits down on it as if he lives there. Tradition says they try everything they know to tip the stranger off that cot, and nothing moves him. Someone runs to fetch the master. The traveler is Guru Gobind Singh. The master hurrying home is an ascetic named Madho Das.
screen: `A HERMITAGE AT NANDED.` → `NOBODY SITS ON THE MASTER'S COT.` → `A STRANGER SITS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Madho Das was a Bairagi, a renunciant, someone who had let go of attachment. He had left home and family behind, lived as a holy man, and gathered his own followers; tradition says people feared his powers. Picture him arriving, out of breath, at his own door, and finding a man calmly sitting where no one may sit. Tellings vary, but the heart of it is a short exchange. Madho Das asks who this is. The Guru answers, in effect, that it's someone Madho Das already knows. And something in him gives way. He says he is the Guru's banda. The word means servant, even bondsman: not a title anyone would choose to look important. That's the turn the Sikh story cares about. Here was a man who had already given up the world, and the Guru's call was not to give up more, but to come back into it: to carry a household's burdens, a people's troubles, and to serve. In the Sikh telling, the hermit's discipline isn't thrown away. It gets a new direction. Tradition says he takes amrit and becomes Banda Singh, though tellings differ on the name he received. Sikhs also remember him as Bahadur, the brave. But the name that stuck first is the one he gave himself at the cot. The Khalsa's hard years begin with him, and some of them are difficult to hear. Notice that it doesn't begin with a battle. It begins with one man deciding whom he serves.

838.title: Five arrows north
838.hook: tradition says the Guru sent Banda north with five arrows and five Sikhs
838.howItsDone: Sikhs tell how Guru Gobind Singh sent Banda Singh to Punjab with five arrows, five Sikhs and letters to the sangats, and remember the instructions tradition says came with them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hermit at Nanded called himself the Guru's banda. Your line was the servant. Today the servant is sent somewhere.

Five arrows. Not a sword, not a crown, not a treasury. Tradition says that when Guru Gobind Singh sent Banda Singh away from Nanded, toward a Punjab he barely knew, those arrows from the Guru's own quiver went with him. So did five Sikhs to ride beside him, a drum, a banner, and letters from the Guru telling the Sikhs of Punjab to stand with this man. A long road north, and a stranger at the front of it.
screen: `FIVE ARROWS FROM THE GURU'S QUIVER.` → `FIVE SIKHS, A DRUM, A BANNER.` → `A LONG ROAD NORTH.`

segments.voice: Why hand a man arrows instead of an army? Sikh tradition reads them as something closer to a seal than a weapon. Five arrows can't win a war. What they could do was say, to anyone who saw them: the Guru sent me. In Punjab, Banda Singh was unknown. He had spent his life as a holy man in other places, and the Sikhs there had every reason to ask why they should follow him. So he carried signs they would recognize: the arrows, the companions, the Guru's letters. Then there's the number. Five keeps turning up in the Sikh story. Five beloved ones stood up at the first amrit. Five Sikhs ride north here. Tradition doesn't explain every five, and it doesn't need to; some readers take the pattern to say this mission belongs to the Khalsa, not to one man. That fits what the tellings say came with the arrows: instructions. Tradition says the Guru told Banda Singh to keep to truth and a disciplined life, never to set himself up as a Guru, and to remember that he served the Khalsa. Authority was given, and a limit was given in the same breath. Some readers find a habit worth keeping here. When you're trusted with a task, you're trusted with two things: the job, and the reminder of whose job it really is. Banda Singh set out with both. Tomorrow, the road reaches a hard town.

839.title: Samana, 1709
839.hook: Banda's growing army takes Samana, home of those who executed Guru Tegh Bahadur
839.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Samana as an early town taken in Banda Singh Bahadur's campaign, and often discuss it alongside the Gurus' teaching that force may be used only against oppression and never from hatred.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Banda Singh rode north with five arrows, five Sikhs, and the Guru's limits. Your line was five arrows. Today the road reaches a town.

A question with no comfortable answer. If someone had killed a person you loved, and years later you had the power to reach them, what would you call what you did next? In Punjab, people began to gather around Banda Singh: farmers, villagers, Sikhs who had read the Guru's letters. His following grew into an army. And the town it struck early on was Samana. Tradition says Samana was home to the men who had carried out the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU CALL IT?` → `A FOLLOWING BECOMES AN ARMY.` → `THE TOWN IS SAMANA.`

segments.voice: Sikh tellings remember Samana as the place where Banda Singh's campaign began to answer the wrongs done to the Gurus. The town was taken by force. Accounts of that day are harsh, and they don't agree on every detail. That honesty belongs in the story: a path that remembers its own martyrs carefully should remember a fallen town carefully too. So what does justice, not revenge, mean? Start with the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib. Those words, the Mul Mantar, describe the One as nirbhau and nirvair: without fear, and without enmity. Japji, a morning prayer, begins with them. No hatred lives in the One they turn toward, and that sets a hard standard for anyone who picks up a sword in the Guru's name. Here is one way to hear the difference. Revenge looks backward and spreads; it wants the other side to hurt the way you hurt, and it rarely knows when to stop. Justice looks at a specific wrong, aims at the ones responsible, and is meant to end. Sikh tellings hold that the sword is lifted only to stop oppression, not to feed a grudge. Some readers hold Banda Singh's campaign up to that standard and honor it. Others ask hard questions about what happened to ordinary people in the towns that fell. Both are part of how this story is told. What doesn't change is the line the Mul Mantar draws: whatever you do, you are not meant to do it from hatred.

840.title: Chappar Chiri, 1710
840.hook: at Chappar Chiri Banda's forces defeat Wazir Khan, the governor who ordered the Sahibzade's deaths
840.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the battle of Chappar Chiri and the taking of Sirhind as the end of Wazir Khan, who ordered the deaths of the younger Sahibzade, and greet one another with the words that the victory belongs to Waheguru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samana, and nirvair, without enmity. Your line was justice, not revenge. Today the week ends on a field.

Go back, for a moment, to a cold tower in Sirhind. Earlier on this path you sat with Mata Gujri and the Guru's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, held there in the winter, and with the order that ended the boys' lives. The man who gave that order was the governor of Sirhind, Wazir Khan, and Sikh memory kept his name. Now the story arrives at a stretch of open ground outside Sirhind called Chappar Chiri, where Banda Singh's army and Wazir Khan's forces meet.
screen: `A COLD TOWER IN SIRHIND.` → `THE GOVERNOR WHO GAVE THE ORDER.` → `AN OPEN FIELD: CHAPPAR CHIRI.`

segments.voice: Sikh tellings describe a hard fight on that field. Tradition remembers Banda Singh's army as farmers and villagers as much as soldiers, facing a well-armed governor's force. By the end of the day, tradition says, Wazir Khan had fallen, and Sirhind itself was taken after. So the line is two plain words: it came. The answer to that winter order finally came. But listen to what Sikhs say when they greet each other: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh. The Khalsa belongs to Waheguru, and so does the victory. Fateh means victory, and it's also the name of the youngest of those two boys in the tower, Fateh Singh. In the Sikh way of saying it, the victory on the field doesn't belong to Banda Singh. It belongs to Waheguru. And it doesn't give anything back. No battle gives back two boys, or the grandmother who died beside them. That's why the line is it came, and not we won. An ending arrived. It closed one long wait. It didn't erase what was lost. This also closes a week that began with far-off sangats, the letters that kept them close, and a last look at the people around the Gurus. Then a hermit at Nanded became a servant, carried five arrows north, and faced the question of justice at Samana. Today the long wait for Sirhind reaches its end.
screen: `A HARD FIGHT ON AN OPEN FIELD.` · `WAZIR KHAN FALLS; SIRHIND IS TAKEN.` · `THE VICTORY BELONGS TO WAHEGURU.` · `AN ENDING DOESN'T GIVE BACK THE LOST.` · then, large: `IT CAME.`

segments.voice: Think of something you waited a long time for, a diagnosis, an apology, a verdict, a letter, and remember the moment it finally came. Notice what it gave you, and honestly what it couldn't give back, and let both sit side by side without choosing. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out, and let the ending belong to something bigger than you.
